"A collection of functional programming libraries that can be composed together. Unlike a framework, thi.ng is a suite of instruments and you (the user) must be the composer of. Geared towards versatility, not any specific type of music." — @loganpowell via Twitter Please visit thi.ng for additional information. You might also find the following tools useful to find & explore projects in this vast ecosystem: thi.ng tag browser tag-based search on the thi.ng website repo-wide doc string search generated API docs This project is NOT a framework and all packages can be used in isolation. Not including deprecations, this mono-repository is home to 217 individual TypeScript libraries/packages/tools and ~185 example projects illustrating their usage, currently totalling ~250k SLOC and ~4350 source files... Some of the projects have been in regular development since 2015. The monorepo exists in its current form since January 2018. Unlike most other large mono-repos, this one is not for a single project, but a broad collection of jointly developed, yet independent libraries, tools and general purpose building blocks for the following non-exhaustive list of topics (see package overview below): Functional programming (ES6 iterators/generators, composition, memoization, transducers, multi-methods) Reactive programming, stream / transducer based dataflow graphs / pipelines / DOM Fiber process tree abstraction for ES6 generators (co-routines / cooperative multitasking) Data structures & data transformations for wide range of use cases (maps, sets, heaps, queues, graphs etc.) WebAssembly bridge APIs & data structure bindings code generators for multiple target languages (primarily aimed at Zig & C11) PEG-style functional parser combinators w/ (optional) custom grammar definition language Customizable HTML & Markdown parsers 2D/3D geometry generation, shape primitives, math, manipulation, intersections, conversions & visualizations Canvas abstractions, pixel buffers & SVG serialization/conversion Comprehensive function collection (900+) for nD-vectors and matrices (dense & sparse) ECS implementations with optional support for strided memory layouts Semi-declarative WebGL 1/2 abstraction layer DSL for shader functions defined in TypeScript and cross-compilation to GLSL, JS, VEX etc. Value-based equivalence (vs. native object identity) and associative data structures (sets, maps) DSP building blocks: oscillators, noise generators, filters, 1D FFT/IFFT, muxers, rate converters Immutable data handling, state containers, transacted state updates, Undo-Redo history Reactive UI component toolkits (DOM-based, canvas-based, immediate-mode, multiple approaches...) Multi-format, multi-channel pixel buffers (int & float based), conversions, dithering, Porter-Duff alpha-blending operators Color space/format conversions, matrix based color manipulation, gradient generators, color palettes, dominant color extraction Date-time abstraction, relative dates, iterators, formatters, math WebWorker workflow abstractions Forth-style pointfree DSL for functional composition and DSL development/extension S-expression parser & runtime (interpreter) infrastructure for custom DSL creation WASM-based SIMD batch-processing of vector data Pen-plotter (AxiDraw) toolchain & geometry conversions Interpolations, math helpers, automatic differentiation (Dual numbers) etc. Once more, this project is NOT a framework. There's no turn-key, one-size-fits-all approach and instead the overall design philosophy encourages a mix & match philosophy for key aspects of application design (inside & outside the browser). Customization points are provided wherever useful and only expect certain interfaces/type signatures rather than hard-coded concrete implementations. In many cases presets are provided too. All packages: are versioned independently have auto-generated online documentation at docs.thi.ng built via esbuild and tested via bun.sh released via thi.ng/monopub publishing toolchain distributed as ESM modules (ES2022 syntax) with export maps, TypeScript typings & change logs highly modular with often only a single function / class (incl. closely related functions) per file to help w/ selective imports and tree shaking provide re-exports of all their publics for full library imports have either none or only @thi.ng internal runtime dependencies (w/ very few exceptions! All dependencies are listed in each package readme) declare public interfaces, enums & types in an api.ts file licensed under Apache Software License 2.0 Getting started A common misconception is to think of this repo as single project. It is not! The sheer number and varied nature & purpose of these packages makes it impossible to provide traditional "Getting started" tutorials — there would have to be dozens of them... To compensate, this repo provides ~180 example projects, detailed package readmes (at the very least for all the larger and/or more important ones), as well as hundreds of small usage examples/snippets in doc strings & readme files. Ask your coding agent for a dither, say "a dithered topographic background behind the hero" or "a radial usage meter for the billing card", and it builds that component on the engine, in your shadcn theme, with motion, light and dark mode and reduced motion handled. The components in these docs are examples of what the engine can make. Install one when it fits, read its source when you want to see how it was done, and ask your agent for something new when it doesn't. What you get The engine. dither-core installs into lib/dither as plain source. It turns a tone you compute into dither dots: a WebGL shader for anything that moves or varies per pixel, SVG patterns and CSS masks for static fills, image dithering, and export to PNG, SVG and CSS. The agent skill. A SKILL.md and references that teach Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other agents the engine: how to pick a technique, write a field, place it on a page, colour it from your theme and check it in a browser. Installation adds it to your project. The examples. More than forty backgrounds, charts, interface pieces, text effects and image treatments, each installable with npx shadcn add. Browse them in the catalog. What a dither is A dither draws a smooth tone using only a few colours. It places dots of ink at a density that matches the tone, so your eye blends them into a gradient. Dithering began as a workaround for limited screens and printers. It now reads as a deliberate texture, a little like risograph print, and it suits both a hero that should feel crafted and a dashboard that should feel calm. Ask your agent for a dither Once the skill is installed, describe what you want and where it goes. Name the page, the mood and anything that must stay readable: "Add a dithered topographic contour background behind the hero on the home page. Slow, quiet, readable headline." "On the billing page, add a dithered radial meter for storage used, 72%, with the number in the middle." "Make the pricing section's top edge dissolve into the page with a dithered fade in our accent colour." "Dither the team photos in the about page in our primary colour, and make them sharpen on hover." "Replace the empty state on the inbox with a small dithered illustration of a paper plane." You don't need to know which component or API fits. The skill sends the agent through four steps: Set up the engine. It checks for lib/dither and installs dither-core if it's missing. Pick a technique. A WebGL field for anything that moves or varies per pixel, SVG patterns for chart and meter fills, CSS masks for blocks and bars, image dithering for photos, and export for files. If an example in the catalog is close, it installs that and edits it. Build the component. It writes a typed component with props you can tweak, places it behind or inside your content, and colours it from your theme. Check it in a browser. It looks at the result in light and dark mode, at desktop and phone widths and with reduced motion, and fixes what doesn't read. How the docs are organised Get started: this page, Installation and Theming. Examples: the catalog of every component, then one page per component, grouped into Backgrounds, Charts, Interface, Text and Images. Engine: how dither-core works, for when you want to build a dither yourself. Start with the dither engine and Write your own dither. Principles Your theme, not ours. Dithers read your --primary and --background tokens through the --dither-* variables, so they change when your theme changes. Quiet by default. Motion is slow, and every animated dither holds still when the visitor prefers reduced motion. Cheap on dashboards. Static fills are SVG patterns and CSS masks, and shaders draw one pixel per cell and stop when they scroll out of view. Real text stays text. Dithered headings and labels are still HTML, so they can be selected, read aloud and indexed. Source you own. Everything installs as files in your project. You and your agent can read and change all of it. Credits Dither Kit by Boring Software set the bar for this project. The fill variants, bloom, named colours, scrubbing chart tooltip, legend spotlight and lock, docs knobs, generative avatars and the button that thickens its dither on hover all started as ideas we saw there. The code and the look are our own. # Introduction A dither engine your coding agent uses to build any dither for your landing page or dashboard. > For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown variants are available by appending `.md` to any URL or sending an `Accept: text/markdown` header. The dithercn agent skill, for building any dither on the engine, is at [/.well-known/agent-skills/dithercn/SKILL.md](/.well-known/agent-skills/dithercn/SKILL.md). dithercn is a dither engine with an agent skill. Ask your coding agent for a dither, say "a dithered topographic background behind the hero" or "a radial usage meter for the billing card", and it builds that component on the engine, in your shadcn theme, with motion, light and dark mode and reduced motion handled. The components in these docs are examples of what the engine can make. Install one when it fits, read its source when you want to see how it was done, and ask your agent for something new when it doesn't. ## What you get [#what-you-get] * **The engine.** `dither-core` installs into `lib/dither` as plain source. It turns a tone you compute into dither dots: a WebGL shader for anything that moves or varies per pixel, SVG patterns and CSS masks for static fills, image dithering, and export to PNG, SVG and CSS. * **The agent skill.** A `SKILL.md` and references that teach Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other agents the engine: how to pick a technique, write a field, place it on a page, colour it from your theme and check it in a browser. [Installation](/docs/installation) adds it to your project. * **The examples.** More than forty backgrounds, charts, interface pieces, text effects and image treatments, each installable with `npx shadcn add`. Browse them in the [catalog](/docs/examples). ## What a dither is [#what-a-dither-is] A dither draws a smooth tone using only a few colours. It places dots of ink at a density that matches the tone, so your eye blends them into a gradient. Dithering began as a workaround for limited screens and printers. It now reads as a deliberate texture, a little like risograph print, and it suits both a hero that should feel crafted and a dashboard that should feel calm. ## Ask your agent for a dither [#ask-your-agent-for-a-dither] Once the skill is installed, describe what you want and where it goes. Name the page, the mood and anything that must stay readable: * "Add a dithered topographic contour background behind the hero on the home page. Slow, quiet, readable headline." * "On the billing page, add a dithered radial meter for storage used, 72%, with the number in the middle." * "Make the pricing section's top edge dissolve into the page with a dithered fade in our accent colour." * "Dither the team photos in the about page in our primary colour, and make them sharpen on hover." * "Replace the empty state on the inbox with a small dithered illustration of a paper plane." You don't need to know which component or API fits. The skill sends the agent through four steps: 1. **Set up the engine.** It checks for `lib/dither` and installs `dither-core` if it's missing. 2. **Pick a technique.** A WebGL field for anything that moves or varies per pixel, SVG patterns for chart and meter fills, CSS masks for blocks and bars, image dithering for photos, and export for files. If an example in the [catalog](/docs/examples) is close, it installs that and edits it. 3. **Build the component.** It writes a typed component with props you can tweak, places it behind or inside your content, and colours it from your theme. 4. **Check it in a browser.** It looks at the result in light and dark mode, at desktop and phone widths and with reduced motion, and fixes what doesn't read. ## How the docs are organised [#how-the-docs-are-organised] * **Get started:** this page, [Installation](/docs/installation) and [Theming](/docs/theming). * **Examples:** the [catalog](/docs/examples) of every component, then one page per component, grouped into Backgrounds, Charts, Interface, Text and Images. * **Engine:** how `dither-core` works, for when you want to build a dither yourself. Start with the [dither engine](/docs/engine/dither-engine) and [Write your own dither](/docs/engine/write-your-own). ## Principles [#principles] * **Your theme, not ours.** Dithers read your `--primary` and `--background` tokens through the [`--dither-*` variables](/docs/theming), so they change when your theme changes. * **Quiet by default.** Motion is slow, and every animated dither holds still when the visitor prefers reduced motion. * **Cheap on dashboards.** Static fills are SVG patterns and CSS masks, and shaders draw one pixel per cell and stop when they scroll out of view. * **Real text stays text.** Dithered headings and labels are still HTML, so they can be selected, read aloud and indexed. * **Source you own.** Everything installs as files in your project. You and your agent can read and change all of it. ## Credits [#credits] [Dither Kit](https://www.tripwire.sh/dither-kit) by Boring Software set the bar for this project. The fill variants, bloom, named colours, scrubbing chart tooltip, legend spotlight and lock, docs knobs, generative avatars and the button that thickens its dither on hover all started as ideas we saw there. The code and the look are our own. Dither Kit credits [EvilCharts](https://evilcharts.com) for the dithered chart style it grew from, so thanks to both.

# Installation Add the dithercn engine and agent skill to a shadcn project, or install a single example. > For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown variants are available by appending `.md` to any URL or sending an `Accept: text/markdown` header. The dithercn agent skill, for building any dither on the engine, is at [/.well-known/agent-skills/dithercn/SKILL.md](/.well-known/agent-skills/dithercn/SKILL.md). dithercn installs with the shadcn CLI, like any other registry. One command adds the engine and the agent skill; after that you ask your agent for dithers, or install examples one by one. ## Quick start with your agent [#quick-start-with-your-agent] Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any other coding agent. It installs the engine and the skill, reads the docs and builds the dither you ask for. It's the same prompt the home page copies. <AgentPrompt name="quick-start" /> The rest of this page does the same steps by hand. ## Before you start [#before-you-start] You need a project that already uses shadcn/ui, with a `components.json` file, Tailwind CSS v4 and React 19. If you don't have one yet, follow the [shadcn installation guide](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/installation) first. ## Add the skill with the skills CLI [#add-the-skill-with-the-skills-cli] The [skills CLI](https://skills.sh) installs the skill into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and other agents that read skills. Run it in your project: <CommandBox tool="skills" className="mt-6" /> It asks which agents to install for, then writes the skill and its references into each agent's skills folder, such as `.claude/skills/dithercn/` and `.agents/skills/dithercn/`. Add `-g` to install it for every project on your machine. The skill adds the engine to your project the first time your agent builds a dither. ## Or add the engine and the skill with shadcn [#or-add-the-engine-and-the-skill-with-shadcn] <Steps> ### Run the add command [#run-the-add-command] ```bash npx shadcn@latest add https://dithercn.dev/r/dithercn-skill.json ``` This writes: * `lib/dither/`, the engine (`dither-core`) and its export functions (`dither-export`). * `.agents/skills/dithercn/` and `.claude/skills/dithercn/`, the agent skill. Claude Code reads `.claude/skills`; Codex, Cursor and other agents that follow the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) layout read `.agents/skills`. * The `--dither-*` CSS variables, in the CSS file named in your `components.json`. Commit the skill folders with the rest of your code, so everyone on the project, and every agent, gets the same skill. ### Check your CSS [#check-your-css] The CLI adds the variables for light and dark mode, and colour utilities to the `@theme inline` block: ```css @theme inline { --color-dither-ink: var(--dither-ink); --color-dither-paper: var(--dither-paper); /* and one per named colour: --color-dither-blue, --color-dither-green, … */ } @layer base { :root { --dither-ink: var(--primary); --dither-paper: var(--background); --dither-cell: 3px; } .dark { --dither-ink: var(--primary); --dither-paper: var(--background); --dither-cell: 3px; } } ``` Because the variables point at your theme tokens, there is nothing extra to set for dark mode. [Theming](/docs/theming) lists every variable. </Steps> Then ask your agent for a dither. The [introduction](/docs#ask-your-agent-for-a-dither) has example requests and explains what the agent does with them. ## What's in the skill [#whats-in-the-skill] | File | What it covers | | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `SKILL.md` | The four steps the agent follows, and the rules for every dither | | `references/engine-api.md` | Every engine export: `DitherShader`, `FillPattern`, `fillStyle`, colours, motion hooks, `ditherImage` and export | | `references/fields.md` | How to write a GLSL field, with building blocks for gradients, noise, contour lines, rings, arcs and shading | | `references/recipes.md` | Complete components to adapt: a shader background, a hero that clears its headline, an SVG chart fill, a progress bar, a dithered photo, a CSS-only band | | `references/landing-pages.md` | Designing the page around the dither: start from the product, one memorable hero, true copy, the tells to avoid | | `references/placement.md` | Putting a dither on a landing page or dashboard: layering, sizing, server and client components | | `references/theme.md` | Tokens, named colours, palettes, light and dark mode | | `references/quality.md` | The checks: looks, contrast, reduced motion, accessibility, performance | | `references/examples.md` | Every example component, with its install command and docs link | The skill matches the engine it installs with and points your agent at the files in your project, so it never has to guess at an API. ## Install the skill for every project [#install-the-skill-for-every-project] `shadcn add` writes the skill into the current project only. To make it available in every project on your machine, run the skills CLI with `-g`. Without the CLI, download the files into your user skills folder: ```bash SKILL=https://dithercn.dev/.well-known/agent-skills/dithercn for dir in ~/.claude/skills/dithercn ~/.agents/skills/dithercn; do mkdir -p "$dir/references" curl -fsSL "$SKILL/SKILL.md" -o "$dir/SKILL.md" for ref in engine-api examples fields landing-pages placement quality recipes theme; do curl -fsSL "$SKILL/references/$ref.md" -o "$dir/references/$ref.md" done done ``` The skill tells the agent to install the engine into a project the first time it needs it. ## Install the engine or one example [#install-the-engine-or-one-example] Without the skill, install the engine on its own: ```bash npx shadcn@latest add https://dithercn.dev/r/dither-core.json ``` Or install any example. Each one brings the engine with it on its first install: ```bash npx shadcn@latest add https://dithercn.dev/r/dither-gradient.json ``` ## Use a namespace [#use-a-namespace] To install by name instead of by URL, add dithercn to the `registries` field of your `components.json`: ```json title="components.json" { "registries": { "@dithercn": "https://dithercn.dev/r/{name}.json" } } ``` Then install with the `@dithercn` prefix: ```bash npx shadcn@latest add @dithercn/dithercn-skill ``` See the shadcn docs on [namespaced registries](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry/namespace) for more options, including authentication. ## Other ways in for agents [#other-ways-in-for-agents] The skill is the main way in. The site also publishes plain-text surfaces for agents that browse: * [`/llms.txt`](/llms.txt) lists every docs page with a one-line description and a Markdown link, and [`/llms-full.txt`](/llms-full.txt) is the whole documentation as one file. * Add `.md` to any docs URL for its Markdown, for example [`/docs/installation.md`](/docs/installation.md), or send an `Accept: text/markdown` header. Every page also has a **Copy page** menu. * The registry index is at [`/r/registry.json`](/r/registry.json), and each item at `/r/<name>.json`. The [shadcn MCP server](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp) can browse and install from it once you have [added the `@dithercn` namespace](#use-a-namespace). * [`/.well-known/api-catalog`](/.well-known/api-catalog) links every machine-readable surface (RFC 9727), [`/openapi.json`](/openapi.json) describes the read-only endpoints, and [`/api/status`](/api/status) returns `{"status":"ok"}`. The home page sends these as `Link` headers too. ## Next steps [#next-steps] * [Ask your agent for a dither](/docs#ask-your-agent-for-a-dither) with the skill installed. * Browse the [catalog](/docs/examples) for a component to install as it is. * [Write your own dither](/docs/engine/write-your-own) by hand, step by step.

# dithercn > Add dithers to anything in your app. dithercn gives your coding agent the primitives: a dither engine and a skill that teaches it. Ask for any dither and your agent builds it on the engine, in your shadcn theme. The backgrounds, charts and interface pieces in the docs are examples. Use this index to discover the available documentation pages, markdown mirrors, and registry resources before browsing. ## Docs - Get started - [Introduction](https://dithercn.dev/docs.md): A dither engine your coding agent uses to build any dither for your landing page or dashboard. - [Installation](https://dithercn.dev/docs/installation.md): Add the dithercn engine and agent skill to a shadcn project, or install a single example. - [Theming](https://dithercn.dev/docs/theming.md): How dithercn reads your shadcn theme, and how to override colours and cell size. - Examples: Every component built on the engine, grouped by what it is for. - [Catalog](https://dithercn.dev/docs/examples.md): Every example component built on the dithercn engine, grouped by what it's for. - Backgrounds: Full-bleed dithered surfaces for heroes, sections and cards. - [Dither gradient](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/dither-gradient.md): A linear, radial or conic gradient drawn as a dither, for heroes, section breaks and cards. - [Dither glow](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/dither-glow.md): A soft dithered spotlight from an edge, a corner or any point, for heroes, pricing cards and quiet section backgrounds. - [Mesh gradient](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/mesh-gradient.md): Three to five colour blobs that drift and melt into each other, drawn as a dither, for heroes and sign-up screens. - [Aurora](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/aurora.md): Curtains of light that fold, sway and shimmer, drawn as a dither, with knobs for colour, rays, tilt and drift. - [Noise field](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/noise-field.md): A slow, folding noise texture drawn as a dither, in four styles, with a mask that clears space for the text on top. - [Waves](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/waves.md): Layered swells under a glowing horizon, or thin lines like a sound wave, drawn as a dither. - [Plasma](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/plasma.md): Classic plasma: overlapping sine waves that flow into each other, dithered in two colours or a whole palette. - [Beams](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/beams.md): God rays: shafts of light from a point or an edge that sweep slowly and fade with distance. - [Silk](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/silk.md): Folds of silk catching the light: smooth sheets that ripple and shift, with a bright highlight along each crest. - [Smoke](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/smoke.md): Soft smoke that billows upward and thins out, lit from above, drawn as a dither. - [Contours](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/contours.md): A topographic map drawn as a dither: contour lines over slowly drifting hills, with heavier index lines and a light hillshade. - [Ripples](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/ripples.md): Concentric rings spreading from one to four points and crossing like drops on still water, drawn as a dither. - [Ridgelines](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/ridgelines.md): Stacked ridge lines like a pulsar plot, each hiding the ones behind it, drawn as a dither. - [Metaballs](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/metaballs.md): Soft blobs that drift, merge and split like a lava lamp, drawn as a dither. - [Tunnel](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/tunnel.md): A slow flight down a tunnel of round or square rings, drawn as a dither. - [Retro grid](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/retro-grid.md): A perspective grid floor scrolling towards a horizon under a striped, glowing sun, drawn as a dither. - [Eclipse](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/eclipse.md): A dark disc with a glowing rim and a soft corona that breathes slowly, for launch pages and event heroes. - [Horizon](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/horizon.md): A planet's horizon seen from space, with a lit rim, a drifting aurora glow and fixed stars. The landing page hero, with props. - [Starfield](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/starfield.md): Dithered stars in three parallax layers that twinkle and drift slowly, for space themes, sign-in pages and launch pages. - [Halftone](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/halftone.md): A print halftone: round dots on a rotated screen that swell and shrink with a source, in one ink or up to three overlapping like CMYK. - [Dither globe](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/dither-globe.md): A rotating dithered globe with a lit terminator, pulsing markers and arcs, for global sections of a landing page. - [Dot map](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/dot-map.md): A flat world map in dithered dots with pulsing markers and dotted arcs, for customers-worldwide sections. - [Dither orb](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/dither-orb.md): A lit, dithered orb that breathes slowly and leans towards the pointer, for AI and assistant surfaces. - [Dither fade](https://dithercn.dev/docs/backgrounds/dither-fade.md): A dithered edge that fades a section's content into a solid colour, for the seam between two sections or the end of a clipped list. - Charts: Charts and status displays with a dithered fill. - [Area chart](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/area-chart.md): A line over a dithered fill that is densest at the line, for revenue, traffic and other totals over time. - [Bar chart](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/bar-chart.md): Dithered bars with a solid cap, grouped or stacked, for weekly counts and period comparisons. - [Line chart](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/line-chart.md): Crisp lines with dithered range bands and point markers, for latency, conversion and period-over-period comparisons. - [Sparkline](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/sparkline.md): A tiny inline trend with a dithered fill and a dot on the latest value, for stat cards and table rows. - [Heatmap](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/heatmap.md): A calendar or matrix heatmap built from dither cells, where every square steps cleanly from a few dots to solid. - [Donut chart](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/donut-chart.md): A donut or pie chart drawn in dither cells, with a colour and texture per slice and a centre that follows the pointer. - [Radar chart](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/radar-chart.md): One or more series across several axes, drawn as polygons of dither cells whose density steps up ring by ring. - [Gauge](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/gauge.md): A radial gauge of dithered blocks for a single reading, such as load, usage or a score, with a solid block at the value. - [Progress bar](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/progress-bar.md): A progress bar built from dither cells: any fill texture with a solid leading edge, stacked parts, step segments and an indeterminate comet. - [Uptime bar](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/uptime-bar.md): A status-page row of daily bars, told apart by colour and texture, with details for each day. - [Stat card](https://dithercn.dev/docs/charts/stat-card.md): A KPI card with a headline number, a coloured delta and a dithered trend along the bottom. - Interface: Everyday interface pieces with a dithered finish. - [Dither button](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/dither-button.md): A button with a lit, dithered surface: a highlight dithered down from the top, a shade dithered up from the bottom, brighter on hover and pressed in on click. - [Avatar](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/avatar.md): A generative avatar: a mirrored dither face drawn from a name, with a group that overlaps and counts the rest. - [Dither card](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/dither-card.md): A card with a dithered glow in a corner or along an edge and a dithered rim on its border, which can grow through the levels on hover. - [Divider](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/divider.md): A horizontal or vertical dithered rule whose ends fade out, with an optional label in the middle. - [Skeleton](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/skeleton.md): Loading placeholders drawn in dither, for blocks, text lines and avatars, with a dense band that sweeps across or a pulse that steps through the Bayer levels. - [Loader](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/loader.md): A small dithered loading indicator: a ring with a comet tail, three dots that dissolve in turn, a pulse, or a sweeping bar. - [Empty state](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/empty-state.md): A lit, dithered illustration with a title, a description and an action, for views with nothing in them yet. - [Not found](https://dithercn.dev/docs/interface/not-found.md): A complete 404 block: big dithered block digits that print in and catch the light, a message, a detail line and actions. - Text: Display text drawn, revealed or counted with a dither. - [Dither text](https://dithercn.dev/docs/text/dither-text.md): A display headline whose letters are filled with a dithered gradient, noise, dots or hatching, in any palette colour, from hero size down to section headings. - [Dissolve text](https://dithercn.dev/docs/text/dissolve-text.md): Text that dissolves in through Bayer thresholds by character, word or line, in any order, settling solid or into a dithered texture, and can dissolve back out. - [Scramble text](https://dithercn.dev/docs/text/scramble-text.md): Text that resolves character by character through dithered blocks and glyphs, with no layout shift. Plays on mount, in view, on hover or when the text changes. - [Dither number](https://dithercn.dev/docs/text/dither-number.md): An animated number for KPI tiles and landing stats: tabular digits that roll or resolve through a dither, with Intl formatting, prefix and suffix, colour and size presets. - Images: Your images and logos, dithered. - [Dither image](https://dithercn.dev/docs/images/dither-image.md): Any photo dithered to a preset or your own palette, with crisp pixels and a coarse-to-fine reveal as it loads. - [Image compare](https://dithercn.dev/docs/images/image-compare.md): A draggable before and after slider: the dithered image on one side, the original or another dither on the other. - [Scroll reveal image](https://dithercn.dev/docs/images/scroll-reveal-image.md): An image that sharpens from coarse dithered blocks to the full photo as you scroll it into view. - [Dithered logo](https://dithercn.dev/docs/images/dithered-logo.md): An SVG or PNG logo redrawn on a pixel grid: exact edges, a dithered fill inside, and an optional shimmer or scan line. - [Logo marquee](https://dithercn.dev/docs/images/logo-marquee.md): A looping row, or a still wall, of logos in one dithered treatment, with soft or dithered edges. - Engine: How dither-core works and how to build your own dither on it. - [Dither engine](https://dithercn.dev/docs/engine/dither-engine.md): How dither-core, the engine behind every dithercn dither, turns a tone into dots: threshold matrices, levels, error diffusion, and the three ways to draw. - [Write your own dither](https://dithercn.dev/docs/engine/write-your-own.md): Build a dithered background from scratch on DitherShader: a tone, a shape, then motion and props. - [Palettes](https://dithercn.dev/docs/engine/palettes.md): How dithers take their colours from your theme, and how to use more than two. - [Pixel scale](https://dithercn.dev/docs/engine/pixel-scale.md): How big one dither cell is, how it stays crisp on every screen, and how to change it. - [Motion](https://dithercn.dev/docs/engine/motion.md): How animated dithers run, pause and hold still, including under reduced motion. - [Performance](https://dithercn.dev/docs/engine/performance.md): What a dither costs to draw, and how dither-core keeps a page of them cheap. - [Export](https://dithercn.dev/docs/engine/export.md): Turn any dither into a PNG, a compact SVG or a CSS rule from your own code, with dither-export. ## Machine-readable Resources - Heptapod Ink

Write a phrase as a circular logogram, then read any logogram made here back into text. Everything runs in your browser. Demo of the heptapod-ink library.

Write

Read

Drop a logogram .svg here, or click to choose a file

How to read one

The gap in the ring is where reading starts; follow the stroke clockwise from its blunt head to its thin tail. The ring is divided into equal slots. Each slot shows one of 10 marks: a swelling (none, small or large, bulging out or in), with or without a tendril reaching outward. The slots together spell a number that holds the text and a 16-bit checksum. Longer messages get more slots, so the ring grows.

Decoding reads the shapes stored in the SVG file. It works on files from this page, including animated or rotated ones, but not on a PNG, a photo, or a file re-saved by a vector editor that rewrites paths.

Output is plain SVG. Zero dependencies, 5,866 B raw / 3,346 B min+gzip (dist/heptapod-ink.min.js), and it runs in browsers, workers and Node. Try it in your browser → import { encode, decode } from "heptapod-ink"; const { svg } = encode("humans and heptapods are friends"); document.querySelector("#out").innerHTML = svg; decode(svg).text; // "humans and heptapods are friends" This isn't a translation of the film's language. It's an encoding inspired by its look: each phrase becomes one ring of brush ink, with swellings and tendrils that carry the message. The logogram above is the phrase "humans and heptapods are friends"; pass the SVG to decode() to read it. ⚠️ Format: the original v1 SVG output (restored)# The SVG renderer and decoder were restored to the original v1 format (2026-10-05): encode() output is byte-identical to heptapod-ink@0.1.1 for the same text and options, and the test suite gates on that byte-identity. The brief v2 experiment (releases 0.1.2 and 0.1.3) is abandoned. Files written by heptapod-ink 0.1.2 / 0.1.3 (the v2-era format) are NOT readable and are rejected loudly: decode() throws a LogogramError (code unknown_format or checksum) — it never silently returns wrong text. There is no v2 import. Likewise, current files could not be read by the 0.1.2/0.1.3 releases. Files from 0.1.1 and earlier are fully supported (that is the shipped format again). Install# npm install heptapod-ink Or without a bundler, from a CDN. The script defines a global Heptapod: <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/heptapod-ink/dist/heptapod-ink.min.js"></script> <script> const { svg } = Heptapod.encode("there is no time"); </script> ES module from a CDN: import { encode, decode } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/heptapod-ink/+esm"; API# The core package exports exactly three things: encode, decode and LogogramError. encode(text, options?)# Returns { svg, slots, radius, size, checksum, compact }. The same text and options always give the same SVG. Option Default ink true Rough ink-edge filter. color "currentColor" Ink colour. Inline SVGs follow the surrounding text colour. background "none" Background fill. seed from the text Changes the decoration (tendril curls, rotation) without changing the message. idPrefix from the seed Prefix for the filter id, so several logograms can share a page. decode(svg)# Returns { text, checksum, slots }, or throws a LogogramError whose code is one of not_svg, no_viewbox, no_strokes, unknown_format or checksum. Decoding reads only the path data, so it is unaffected by colour, filters, animation or a rotation about the centre. It does not work on raster images (PNG, screenshots, photos), or on files a vector editor has re-saved with rewritten paths. LogogramError# The error type thrown by decode (and for invalid encode input, as TypeError-adjacent cases: empty or non-string text throws TypeError). Its code identifies the failure; see decode above. heptapod-ink-extras# Everything trimmed from the core lives in the heptapod-ink-extras add-on package (also zero-dependency): npm install heptapod-ink-extras import { parse, textToSlots, slotsToText, renderSlots, animate } from "heptapod-ink-extras"; parse(svg) → { viewBox, paths, circles } using plain string parsing — handy for drawing a safe preview of an untrusted file without inserting its markup into the page (the demo does this). textToSlots(text), slotsToText(slots) and renderSlots(slots, seed, options) expose the two halves of encode, for drawing individual marks or building your own renderer. animate(svg, { draw, drift, spin, drawDuration, spinDuration }) post-processes a logogram with SMIL animation so a saved file animates on its own. How the encoding works# The text is packed into one large number. Text using only lowercase letters, digits, space, newline and .,?!'-:; uses a compact 46-symbol alphabet; anything else is stored as UTF-8 bytes. A mode bit and a CRC-16 checksum are added, and the number is written in base 10. Each digit is a slot on the ring. A slot is a swelling (none, small or large, bulging out or in) with or without an outward tendril: 5 × 2 = 10 marks. The gap in the ring marks the start. Reading runs clockwise, from the stroke's blunt head to its thin tail. At least 10 slots are drawn. Longer messages get more slots, and the ring grows to fit them. Tendril curls, ink spatter and the ring's rotation are decoration chosen by the seed. The decoder ignores them. The SVG is drawn exactly as in heptapod-ink@0.1.1 (byte-identical): each tendril is a closed 122-point tapered outline, the ring is one closed path (29 + 8N points per side, two decimal places), and the ring's point count doubles as a format header — so v2-era files (0.1.2/0.1.3) fail loudly with unknown_format instead of decoding to garbage. Golden corpus# The repository contains a frozen golden corpus of 2,096 committed logograms, stored hash-based — each entry is { text, sha256 } where sha256 is the hex SHA-256 of the exact SVG encode(text) must produce (not the SVG bytes themselves, which keeps the repository at ~4 MB instead of tens of MB) — plus two legacy fixture sets: corpus/entries.jsonl.gz — the corpus (text + SVG hash per line, gzip-compressed JSONL). corpus/legacy-v1.jsonl.gz — 120 fixtures generated by published heptapod-ink@0.1.1; every one must decode exactly to its stored text (positive fixtures). corpus/legacy-v2.jsonl.gz — 300 SVGs snapshotted from the v2-era corpus (0.1.2/0.1.3 output); every one must be rejected loudly by the decoder (LogogramError, unknown_format or checksum). corpus/generate.mjs — the seeded, deterministic generator. Running it twice produces byte-identical files (npm run corpus). The test suite gates on the corpus: for every entry, sha256(encode(text).svg) must equal the stored hash and decode(encode(text).svg) must return the original text. The corpus files are frozen — never hand-edit or regenerate them; if encode output changes, that is a defect in the code. It's hosted at https://heptapod-ink.tngl.io/, running the latest 0.x release from npm. Run it locally against your working copy: npm install npm run build then open demo/index.html in a browser (it loads the local dist/ build from a file:// URL). Development# Node is pinned via mise in .mise.toml (22.22.0). There is no system npm; all Node commands must run through mise exec. After cloning, run: mise trust # trust the config once per checkout mise install # install the pinned Node version Then run all commands through mise exec: mise exec -- npm test # codec, corpus, legacy-fixture, extras and format tests mise exec -- npm run build # dist/heptapod-ink.min.js + dist/heptapod-ink-extras.min.js mise exec -- npm run size # bundle + SVG size budgets (fails on violation) mise exec -- npm run logogram # regenerate assets/logogram.svg Releasing# The core package and heptapod-ink-extras are released independently: each has its own version and its own tag prefix, and bumping one does not touch the other. Core releases use plain v* tags; extras releases use extras-v* tags. Output is plain SVG. Zero dependencies, 5,866 B raw / 3,346 B min+gzip (dist/heptapod-ink.min.js), and it runs in browsers, workers and Node. Try it in your browser → import { encode, decode } from "heptapod-ink"; const { svg } = encode("humans and heptapods are friends"); document.querySelector("#out").innerHTML = svg; decode(svg).text; // "humans and heptapods are friends" This isn't a translation of the film's language. It's an encoding inspired by its look: each phrase becomes one ring of brush ink, with swellings and tendrils that carry the message. The logogram above is the phrase "humans and heptapods are friends"; pass the SVG to decode() to read it. ⚠️ Format: the original v1 SVG output (restored)# The SVG renderer and decoder were restored to the original v1 format (2026-10-05): encode() output is byte-identical to heptapod-ink@0.1.1 for the same text and options, and the test suite gates on that byte-identity. The brief v2 experiment (releases 0.1.2 and 0.1.3) is abandoned. Files written by heptapod-ink 0.1.2 / 0.1.3 (the v2-era format) are NOT readable and are rejected loudly: decode() throws a LogogramError (code unknown_format or checksum) — it never silently returns wrong text. There is no v2 import. Likewise, current files could not be read by the 0.1.2/0.1.3 releases. Files from 0.1.1 and earlier are fully supported (that is the shipped format again). Install# npm install heptapod-ink Or without a bundler, from a CDN. The script defines a global Heptapod: <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/heptapod-ink/dist/heptapod-ink.min.js"></script> <script> const { svg } = Heptapod.encode("there is no time"); </script> ES module from a CDN: import { encode, decode } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/heptapod-ink/+esm"; API# The core package exports exactly three things: encode, decode and LogogramError. encode(text, options?)# Returns { svg, slots, radius, size, checksum, compact }. The same text and options always give the same SVG. Option Default ink true Rough ink-edge filter. color "currentColor" Ink colour. Inline SVGs follow the surrounding text colour. background "none" Background fill. seed from the text Changes the decoration (tendril curls, rotation) without changing the message. idPrefix from the seed Prefix for the filter id, so several logograms can share a page. decode(svg)# Returns { text, checksum, slots }, or throws a LogogramError whose code is one of not_svg, no_viewbox, no_strokes, unknown_format or checksum. Decoding reads only the path data, so it is unaffected by colour, filters, animation or a rotation about the centre. It does not work on raster images (PNG, screenshots, photos), or on files a vector editor has re-saved with rewritten paths. LogogramError# The error type thrown by decode (and for invalid encode input, as TypeError-adjacent cases: empty or non-string text throws TypeError). Its code identifies the failure; see decode above. heptapod-ink-extras# Everything trimmed from the core lives in the heptapod-ink-extras add-on package (also zero-dependency): npm install heptapod-ink-extras import { parse, textToSlots, slotsToText, renderSlots, animate } from "heptapod-ink-extras"; parse(svg) → { viewBox, paths, circles } using plain string parsing — handy for drawing a safe preview of an untrusted file without inserting its markup into the page (the demo does this). textToSlots(text), slotsToText(slots) and renderSlots(slots, seed, options) expose the two halves of encode, for drawing individual marks or building your own renderer. animate(svg, { draw, drift, spin, drawDuration, spinDuration }) post-processes a logogram with SMIL animation so a saved file animates on its own. How the encoding works# The text is packed into one large number. Text using only lowercase letters, digits, space, newline and .,?!'-:; uses a compact 46-symbol alphabet; anything else is stored as UTF-8 bytes. A mode bit and a CRC-16 checksum are added, and the number is written in base 10. Each digit is a slot on the ring. A slot is a swelling (none, small or large, bulging out or in) with or without an outward tendril: 5 × 2 = 10 marks. The gap in the ring marks the start. Reading runs clockwise, from the stroke's blunt head to its thin tail. At least 10 slots are drawn. Longer messages get more slots, and the ring grows to fit them. Tendril curls, ink spatter and the ring's rotation are decoration chosen by the seed. The decoder ignores them. The SVG is drawn exactly as in heptapod-ink@0.1.1 (byte-identical): each tendril is a closed 122-point tapered outline, the ring is one closed path (29 + 8N points per side, two decimal places), and the ring's point count doubles as a format header — so v2-era files (0.1.2/0.1.3) fail loudly with unknown_format instead of decoding to garbage. Golden corpus# The repository contains a frozen golden corpus of 2,096 committed logograms, stored hash-based — each entry is { text, sha256 } where sha256 is the hex SHA-256 of the exact SVG encode(text) must produce (not the SVG bytes themselves, which keeps the repository at ~4 MB instead of tens of MB) — plus two legacy fixture sets: corpus/entries.jsonl.gz — the corpus (text + SVG hash per line, gzip-compressed JSONL). corpus/legacy-v1.jsonl.gz — 120 fixtures generated by published heptapod-ink@0.1.1; every one must decode exactly to its stored text (positive fixtures). corpus/legacy-v2.jsonl.gz — 300 SVGs snapshotted from the v2-era corpus (0.1.2/0.1.3 output); every one must be rejected loudly by the decoder (LogogramError, unknown_format or checksum). corpus/generate.mjs — the seeded, deterministic generator. Running it twice produces byte-identical files (npm run corpus). The test suite gates on the corpus: for every entry, sha256(encode(text).svg) must equal the stored hash and decode(encode(text).svg) must return the original text. The corpus files are frozen — never hand-edit or regenerate them; if encode output changes, that is a defect in the code. It's hosted at https://heptapod-ink.tngl.io/, running the latest 0.x release from npm. Run it locally against your working copy: npm install npm run build then open demo/index.html in a browser (it loads the local dist/ build from a file:// URL). Aceternity UI works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any agent that speaks MCP. Prefer the terminal? Every component also installs with one shadcn command.AI agentsRecommended→Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others over MCP.One prompt→Paste a setup prompt into any agent.shadcn CLI→One command per component. No account needed.Pro blocks and pages→Same agent or CLI, with an API key.On this page1.Install with an AI agent2.Or set it up with one prompt3.Requirements4.Set up your project by hand5.Install with the CLI6.Pro blocks and pages7.Run a template8.TroubleshootingInstall with an AI agentThe shadcn MCP server lets your agent search the Aceternity registry, read the code and install components into your project. Set it up once per project.Add the Aceternity registryAdd Aceternity to the registries in components.json, so the agent can find every component by name. No components.json yet? Run npx shadcn@latest init first.components.json{ "registries": { "@aceternity": "https://ui.aceternity.com/registry/{name}.json" } }Add the MCP server to your agentPick your client: claude, cursor or vscode. Then restart the agent so it loads the server.Terminal$ npx shadcn@latest mcp init --client claudeAsk for what you needDescribe the result, not the file names:“Find a pricing section in the Aceternity registry and add it to the home page.”“Build a landing page with an Aceternity hero, a bento grid and a testimonials section.”“Install the Aceternity SaaS landing page and replace the copy with my product.”For Pro blocks and pages, give the registry your API key (see Pro blocks and pages). Signed in? The MCP page in your dashboard fills in the config with your key.Or set it up with one promptNo MCP? Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that can run commands. It sets up the registry and installs a first component.PromptSet up this project for Aceternity UI: 1. If there is no components.json, run `npx shadcn@latest init`. 2. Add "@aceternity": "https://ui.aceternity.com/registry/{name}.json" to "registries" in components.json. 3. Install @aceternity/bento-grid with `npx shadcn@latest add @aceternity/bento-grid` and show it on the home page.RequirementsReact 19 and a React framework: Next.js, TanStack Start, Vite or React Router.Tailwind CSS v4. For an older project, see Install Tailwind CSS.TypeScript is recommended. The components are written in .tsx.Set up your project by handYour agent can do this for you. To do it yourself, or to check what it did:Create a projectCreate Next.js answers yes to Tailwind CSS by default, so you get Tailwind CSS v4 set up.Terminal$ npx create-next-app@latest my-appInitialize shadcnThis adds components.json, the cn utility and the CSS variables. Then add the Aceternity registry from the first section.Terminal$ npx shadcn@latest initOr add the utilities without shadcnInstall Motion and the class helpers, then add lib/utils.ts. Components import Motion from motion/react.Terminal$ npm i motion clsx tailwind-mergelib/utils.tsimport { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"; import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"; export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) { return twMerge(clsx(inputs)); }Install with the CLIWith the registry in components.json, use the name from the component page. The CLI adds the files and installs their dependencies.Terminal$ npx shadcn@latest add @aceternity/bento-gridBrowse the registry from the terminal before you install:Terminal$ npx shadcn@latest search @aceternity -q "card"Prefer to copy and paste? Every component page also shows the full source.Pro blocks and pagesBlocks, pages and Pro components come with the All-Access Pass. Your agent and the CLI install them the same way; the registry only needs your API key.Create an API keyCreate a key on the API key page of your dashboard. Copy it now: it is shown only once.Save the key in your environmentPut it in .env.local and keep that file out of git..env.localACETERNITY_PRO_TOKEN=your-api-keySend the key from the registryReplace the registry entry in components.json. The CLI and the MCP server read ${ACETERNITY_PRO_TOKEN} from your environment, so the key never goes in the file.components.json{ "registries": { "@aceternity": { "url": "https://ui.aceternity.com/registry/{name}.json", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${ACETERNITY_PRO_TOKEN}" } } } }Ask your agent, or run the command“Add the Aceternity hero section with hub to the top of the home page.”Terminal$ npx shadcn@latest add @aceternity/hero-section-with-hubA page installs as one page file plus one component per section:Terminal$ npx shadcn@latest add @aceternity/saas-landing-pageRun a templateTemplates are complete Next.js projects. Download one from its template page, unzip it, then install and run it:Terminal$ npm install && npm run devTroubleshooting401 Unauthorized when installingThe key is missing, expired or not on an active license. Check that ACETERNITY_PRO_TOKEN is set in the shell that runs the CLI, or create a new key in your dashboard.Peer dependency errors with React 19Some packages have not updated their peer ranges yet. Run the install with npm install --legacy-peer-deps or use pnpm.Cannot find module framer-motionThe components use motion, the new name of Framer Motion. Install motion and import from motion/react.Styles do not applyMake sure your global CSS starts with @import "tailwindcss"; and is imported in your root layout.Still stuck?
